questions.q: Two datasets have the same mean and standard deviation. Why might you still need spatial tools to describe them?
options: They can't have the same mean
They can have completely different spatial patterns, which non-spatial statistics ignore
They need a different level of measurement
questions.why: Attribute statistics ignore location. Maps and centrography describe where values and features are.

questions.q: Percent poverty is strongly skewed, and on an equal interval map most counties land in one class. Why?
options: Equal interval splits the range into equal widths, so skewed data pile into one or two classes
Equal interval puts the same number of counties in each class
The map uses too many classes
Equal interval only works for counts
questions.why: Look at a histogram before choosing a classification method.

questions.q: A quantile map puts the same number of areas in each class. What can go wrong?
options: Very similar values can end up in different classes, or very different values in the same class
questions.why: Quantile maps show relative rank well, but the breaks may not reflect real gaps in the data.

questions.q: Why are natural breaks (Jenks) maps hard to compare across years?
options: The breaks are specific to each dataset
They use a diverging color scheme
questions.why: Breaks placed at gaps in one year's data won't match the next year's.

questions.q: When are manual breaks especially useful?
options: When there are meaningful thresholds, like the federal poverty line or an EPA standard
questions.why: User-defined breaks can match thresholds readers care about, or round, easy-to-read numbers.

questions.q: A county map of the total number of people in poverty mostly shows...
options: where people live, which is why mapping the percent (normalizing) is better
questions.why: Choropleth maps should almost always show rates, percentages or densities, so areas of different sizes can be compared.

questions.q: Large rural counties visually dominate a choropleth map even though fewer people live there. This is...
questions.why: Bigger polygons draw more attention, while small, dense urban units are hard to see.

questions.q: Which color scheme fits a map of population change, from losses through zero to gains?
options: Diverging (two colors with a neutral middle)
questions.why: Diverging schemes suit data with a meaningful midpoint. Sequential schemes suit data that simply go from low to high.

questions.q: A rural tract with a few hundred residents shows an extremely high rate of a rare disease. Why be cautious?
options: Rates for small populations are unstable and can be extreme by chance
It should be mapped as a count
questions.why: Small denominators make rates jump around, and those extreme values stand out on a map.

questions.q: The Census Bureau's mean center of US population is weighted by...
options: the number of people at each location
questions.why: Weighting each location by its population shows where the population is centered. It has moved west and south since 1790.

questions.q: Why might the median center be a better summary than the mean center?
options: It's always in the middle of the map
It's less sensitive to outliers far from the rest of the data
questions.why: Like the regular mean, the mean center can be pulled toward a few distant points.

questions.q: Why should data be in a projected coordinate system before calculating centrography?
options: Latitude and longitude can't be averaged
questions.why: Degrees of longitude change length with latitude. A projection like NC State Plane measures in consistent units.

questions.q: A standard deviational ellipse with a major axis much longer than its minor axis means...
options: the features are elongated in one direction (a directional trend)
questions.why: The ellipse's orientation and axes capture direction, which the standard distance circle can't.

questions.q: For wind turbines built before 2005, the mean center falls in southern Utah, where there are almost no turbines. Why?
options: The turbines were split among separate regions, and the mean center falls between them
The data were in latitude and longitude
questions.why: A mean center doesn't have to fall on or near any actual feature.

questions.q: The North Carolina tornado ellipse is stretched east to west. The reading says this mostly reflects...
options: a real directional trend in tornado tracks
the shape of the state, which is much wider east to west than north to south
questions.why: Features can only occur inside the study area, so its boundary can drive the ellipse's orientation.

options: Why features are arranged that way, or whether the pattern differs from chance
questions.why: Point pattern analysis is needed to compare a pattern to what you'd expect by chance.
